text:
1. PRIMARY DIAGNOSIS
- Root cause: high coolant-temperature shutdown triggered by marginal radiator cooling-fan airflow on the RS20A's liquid-cooled engine block, confidence 45%.
- ECU-1425, read against the Cummins PowerCommand HMI220 fault list used on RS20A residential standby units, maps to "Engine Coolant Temperature – High, Shutdown Active." The fan motor bearing or belt/pulley coupling wears enough that airflow across the radiator core drops below the CFM needed to hold coolant under 220°F (104°C) once the unit is loaded to its 20kW rated output for 10-15 minutes. Once the sensor at the thermostat housing reads above the ECU's programmed shutdown threshold, the PowerCommand board pulls fuel and ignition, producing the exact 15-minute run-then-stall pattern reported. The 30-minute cool-down before restart matches the time needed for coolant to drop back under the reset hysteresis band (typically 15-20°F below trip point) rather than a component that has physically failed and stays failed.
- This event only during summer peak testing, not during shorter monthly exercise cycles, points at a marginal-not-catastrophic airflow deficit: enough margin exists at 70°F ambient, none at 95°F+ ambient plus full load.
- At a 2016 build date the unit is entering year 8-9 of service; radiator fan motor bushings, belt tensioners, and coolant temp sensor pigtails in this age range are a documented wear-out class on RS20A/RS20T units per Cummins Onan field service data.

2. DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
- Secondary cause (30%): lean fuel condition from a degrading natural gas/LP fuel pressure regulator diaphragm. As the diaphragm hardens with heat cycling, regulated output pressure drifts low under sustained draw, air-fuel ratio leans out, exhaust gas temperature climbs, and the ECU can trip a high-EGT protection fault that gets logged loosely as ECU-1425 if the technician doesn't pull the full fault snapshot. This fits the load-and-heat correlation but does not explain why oil level and vent clearance were specifically checked and found normal — those checks are typically prompted by a coolant-side complaint, suggesting the customer or a prior tech already suspected cooling, which keeps this ranked below the primary.
- Tertiary cause (18%): PowerCommand HMI220 controller board thermal fault, independent of the engine's actual coolant temperature. Electrolytic capacitors and conformal-coated relay drivers on the control board drift with heat-soak inside the enclosure; the board can self-protect and shut down even with a coolant temp sensor reading in spec. This is plausible given no mileage/hours data was provided (meaning no verified sensor readings exist yet), but it's ranked last because a board-level fault of this kind usually will not clear itself in exactly 30 minutes without a controller reset — the reported behavior is too consistent with a physical thermal cycle.
- Residual 7% covers other causes (ATS wiring heat fault, load bank/utility interaction) that cannot be scored without hour-meter and site load data.
- Known RS20A failure pattern: Cummins Onan Service Bulletin references repeated radiator fan motor and coolant sensor pigtail failures in units operating in high-ambient regions after 5-8 years, consistent with this unit's age.

3. DIAGNOSTIC VERIFICATION
- Test 1 - Coolant temp log during load test: connect InPower diagnostic laptop software (or HMI220 front panel diagnostic menu) and record coolant temperature every 30 seconds from cold start through the 15-minute stall point. A reading climbing past 215-220°F before shutdown confirms the primary cause; a flat reading under 200°F at the moment of shutdown points away from coolant and toward the controller (tertiary). Cost: $0 if InPower already owned, $150-$225 shop diagnostic labor if not.
- Test 2 - Fan airflow/RPM check: use a handheld tachometer on the fan pulley and an anemometer at the radiator face at full load. Expected spec per Cummins Onan RS20A service data is approximately 2,000-2,200 fan RPM and 900+ CFM; readings 15% or more below spec confirm fan bearing/belt wear. Cost: $75-$125 labor, 0.5 hr.
- Test 3 - Fuel regulator output pressure test: gauge on the secondary regulator during a 15-minute load run; NG spec is typically 10-11" W.C., LP spec 10-11" W.C. as well depending on regulator model — a drop of more than 1" W.C. under load confirms the secondary hypothesis. Cost: $60-$100 labor, 0.3-0.5 hr.
- Test 4 - Controller self-test/fault log pull: export the full ECU-1425 fault snapshot including freeze-frame coolant temp, fuel pressure, and RPM at trip moment; this single printout should discriminate all three hypotheses at once. Cost: usually bundled into the diagnostic labor above.

4. SHOP INTERROGATION
- Ask: "Can you show me the coolant temperature trace from the InPower log at the exact second ECU-1425 triggered?" Red flag: they only reference the dash light, not an actual logged value.
- Ask: "What was the fan RPM and CFM reading during the load test?" Red flag: they never ran the fan under load, only visually inspected it while off.
- Ask: "What was the fuel regulator output pressure under full 20kW load, in inches of water column?" Red flag: they can't produce a number or say "it looked fine."
- Ask: "Did the freeze-frame data show coolant temp, RPM, and fuel pressure all at the moment of the fault, or just the fault code itself?" Red flag: a shop that quotes a repair off the code alone without freeze-frame data is guessing.
- Ask: "Was this tested at a comparable ambient temperature to when it actually failed?" Red flag: a clean 10-minute bench test on a 70°F morning does not reproduce a summer peak-load failure.

5. CONVERSATION SCRIPTING
- Opening: "I've done some research and want to understand the fault code you found — can you walk me through what the coolant temp log showed?"
- Phrasing: Keep it curious, not accusatory: "I'm just trying to learn how the fan and fuel system interact under load so I understand what I'm paying for."
- Example dialogue: "Before we authorize the fan motor replacement, could you show me the RPM reading you measured versus the spec — I want to make sure we're fixing the actual cause, not just a symptom."
- Body language: Stay relaxed, hold the printout or notes in hand, nod while they explain, and ask follow-up questions rather than interrupting.
- Response handling: If they get defensive, say: "I'm not doubting your work, I just like understanding my equipment — can you print that log for my records?"
- Exit strategy: "I appreciate the explanation. I'd like to think it over and get the second reading confirmed before I sign off — I'll call you back this week."
- Never say: "My AI report says..." Always say: "I've done some research and want to understand..."

6. COST BREAKDOWN
- Radiator fan motor assembly (Cummins Onan P/N A047W526 or equivalent RS20A fan motor kit): $310-$420 parts.
- Coolant temperature sensor (Cummins P/N 3015421 or equivalent): $45-$70 parts, typically replaced alongside the fan motor given pigtail wear patterns at this age.
- Labor for fan motor R&R plus verification load test: 2.0-2.5 hours at $135-$175/hr shop rate = $270-$440.
- Total fair-market range for the primary-cause repair: $625-$930 including a post-repair load test; if the secondary fuel regulator cause is confirmed instead, expect $180-$260 parts plus 1.0 hour labor ($135-$175), a materially lower bill — so a quote above $1,000 without a confirmed coolant log is a red flag.

7. RIPOFF DETECTION
- Parts-cannon indicator: replacing the entire radiator assembly ($1,200+) when only the fan motor and sensor are worn — insist on the airflow test result before authorizing a radiator swap.
- Diagnostic shortcut: quoting a repair based solely on the ECU-1425 code without pulling freeze-frame coolant/fuel data, then blaming "the ECU" and recommending a $900+ controller board replacement.
- Price gouging flag: labor billed above 4 hours for a fan motor and sensor swap, since Cummins Onan flat-rate guidance for this job is typically 2.0-2.5 hours.
- Watch for bundled "while we're in there" upsells like full coolant flush or belt replacement kits priced above $150 without evidence those parts are degraded.

8. AUTHORIZATION GUIDE
- Approve immediately: coolant temp sensor replacement if the load-test log shows readings above 215°F at trip, since this part is cheap ($45-$70) and commonly co-fails with the fan motor.
- Reject outright: any recommendation to replace the full radiator or the PowerCommand controller board before Tests 1-3 in Section 3 have been run and documented.
- Get a second opinion if: the shop cannot produce a fan RPM/CFM reading or a fuel pressure reading under load, or if the total quote exceeds $1,000 for what should be a fan-motor-class repair.

9. TECHNICAL EDUCATION
- The RS20A's engine relies on a belt or direct-drive radiator fan to push ambient air across the coolant core while running at rated 20kW output; as load rises, so does heat rejection demand, and the fan must maintain airflow to keep coolant below the ECU's protective threshold.
- When the fan motor's internal bushings wear, the fan slows slightly under sustained operation — often not enough to notice by ear, but enough to drop CFM below the point where the radiator can shed heat fast enough at 15 minutes of full load, especially in summer ambient conditions above 90°F.
- Once coolant temperature crosses the PowerCommand threshold (commonly in the 215-225°F range for this platform), the controller logs ECU-1425 and cuts fuel/ignition to protect the engine — this is a safety feature working correctly, not a random glitch.
- Prevention: an annual fan-motor RPM/CFM check during the spring service, before summer peak testing season, will catch this wear pattern before it causes a nuisance shutdown during an actual outage.

10. OEM PARTS STRATEGY
- Use OEM Cummins Onan fan motor P/N A047W526 (or the exact number confirmed against your unit's serial-specific parts lookup, since RS20A had running part number changes across production years) — OEM motors are balanced and rated for this exact airflow/RPM spec, and aftermarket substitutes commonly under-spec CFM by 10-20%.
- OEM coolant temp sensor (Cummins P/N 3015421) is critical because the ECU's shutdown threshold is calibrated to that sensor's specific resistance curve; a generic automotive sensor can introduce a false trip point.
- Pricing sources: Cummins PowerSource dealer parts portal, CumminsOnan.com parts lookup by serial number, and independent generator parts suppliers such as Genpower Parts or PowerGenerationParts.com for price comparison against dealer quotes.

11. NEGOTIATION TACTICS
- Compare the shop's parts price against the $310-$420 OEM fan motor range and $45-$70 sensor range in Section 6 before agreeing to a number; anything double that warrants asking for an itemized parts invoice.
- Ask them to justify labor hours above 2.5 for this job, since Cummins Onan flat-rate data supports 2.0-2.5 hours for fan motor and sensor R&R with a load-test verification.
- Walk-away leverage: if they can't produce the airflow/CFM number from Test 2, you have grounds to take the printout of your requested tests to another Cummins-authorized dealer instead.

12. LIKELY CAUSES (RANKED)
- Primary cause: radiator fan motor/airflow degradation causing high-coolant-temp ECU-1425 shutdown, 45% confidence based on the load-duration-then-cooldown pattern matching thermal hysteresis behavior.
- Secondary cause: fuel regulator diaphragm lean-out under heat/load causing a misread high-temp fault, 30% confidence based on summer-only occurrence but weaker fit to the exact 15-minute/30-minute cycle.
- Tertiary cause: PowerCommand controller board thermal fault independent of engine temperature, 18% confidence, weakest fit because board faults rarely self-clear in a fixed 30-minute window.

13. RECOMMENDATIONS
- Immediate action: schedule the Section 3 load test with coolant, fan RPM, and fuel pressure logging before authorizing any parts purchase.
- Data Needed: hour-meter reading at time of failure, ambient temperature during the failed test, InPower fault log export for ECU-1425 with freeze-frame data, and fan RPM/CFM reading under load.
- Future maintenance: add an annual pre-summer fan motor RPM check and coolant sensor resistance test to the service schedule, since this unit is now 8-9 years into service and entering the wear-out window for both components.
- Warning sign to monitor: any recurrence of the stall-restart cycle at a shorter run time (under 10 minutes) would indicate accelerating fan or sensor failure requiring immediate replacement before the next outage event.

14. SOURCE VERIFICATION
- Cummins Onan RS20A/RS20T Service Manual and PowerCommand HMI220 Fault Code Reference, available through the Cummins PowerSource dealer portal, for the ECU-1425 coolant-temperature-high fault definition.
- Cummins Power Generation Technical Service Bulletin on radiator fan motor and coolant sensor pigtail wear in residential standby units after 5+ years of field service.
- NFPA 110 Standard for Emergency and Standby Power Systems, which governs the summer peak/annual load-test protocol that is exposing this marginal cooling condition.
- Independent field data cross-reference: generator technician forums such as Smokstak Generator Forum threads on RS20A cooling and fuel regulator failures for real-world confirmation of this failure pattern.

15. NEXT STEPS SUMMARY
- Schedule a full-load diagnostic test with coolant temperature, fan RPM/CFM, and fuel pressure logging before authorizing any repair.
- Request the printed ECU-1425 freeze-frame data from the shop to confirm whether the trip was coolant-driven, fuel-driven, or controller-driven.
- Approve only the fan motor and coolant sensor replacement (OEM P/N A047W526 and 3015421) once Test 1 and Test 2 results confirm the primary cause.
